items.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: and then he began to hire Lionel Hampton and Teddy Wilson

ctx.x: making all the money.” He says, “I’m not making any money.” So and he says, “sometimes I don’t know if they’re playing like me or I’m playing like them.” You know he said kind of things like that, you know? So he really didn’t make too much money because he was you know everybody was trying to stay out of the Army and a lot of musicians beat it because it was a lot of jobs and things then, you know with everybody going in, and the musicians just wasn’t Army material, you know. So I remember one time we were out…

I want to ask you a question about jazz. You know we had talked, and you had talked about this too, how that in the early years of jazz of course before a certain time, like before Benny Goodman, all the bands were pretty much segregated, and then he began to hire Lionel Hampton and Teddy Wilson. But it seemed to me that the music was the one thing that allowed people to go back and forth without all these barriers, you know? Do you see a way that we can use music today to do the same things? Because it seems to…

Be integrated more? Yeah, it should be. Well you know they have it in the smaller groups they don’t have the big bands really to mix it more, with more, because we don’t have big bands. But that’s one thing that they never paid much attention to, you know? Of course © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-
